learning.javascript:
Characters are numbers: ASCII

A computer stores each character as a number, its character code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is the oldest common set of codes. It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

A few landmarks are worth knowing:

  32       space
  48 – 57  '0' to '9'
  65 – 90  'A' to 'Z'
  97 – 122 'a' to 'z'

So 'A' (65) and 'a' (97) are different characters: they're 32 apart. Digits and letters are in order, so subtracting codes gives positions: 'c' minus 'a' is 2.

In JavaScript, s.charCodeAt(i) gives the code of the character at index i, and String.fromCharCode(n) goes the other way:

"a".charCodeAt(0);         // 97
String.fromCharCode(65);   // "A"
for (const c of s) { ... } // c is each character of s, as a 1-character string

Beyond ASCII, JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units: charCodeAt returns a number from 0 to 65535, and some characters (such as many emoji) take two units. See MDN's charCodeAt(). That's why this question sticks to ASCII, where one character is always one unit.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

"Have I seen this before?": hash tables

One way to check for repeats is to compare every character with every other one. That works, but for a string of n characters it takes about n×n comparisons.

A hash table remembers what it has seen. It turns each value into a number, its hash, which picks a slot to store it in. So checking whether a value is already there takes about the same short time however much is stored: constant time on average. (Two values can land in the same slot, which is why it's "on average".) Going through the string once, checking and remembering each character, takes about n steps.

JavaScript's hash table: Set

A Set holds each value at most once:

const seen = new Set();
seen.add("x");
seen.has("x");   // true
seen.has("y");   // false
seen.add("x");   // already there: nothing changes
seen.size;       // 1

The language specification requires that "Set objects must be implemented using either hash tables or other mechanisms that, on average, provide access times that are sublinear on the number of elements in the collection" (ECMAScript, Set Objects). MDN's Set page is a friendlier guide. (A Map is the same idea with a value stored for each key.)

In Python, ord(c) gives the code of a one-character string, and chr(n) goes the other way:

ord("a")      # 97
chr(65)       # "A"
for c in s:   # c is each character of s, as a 1-character string
    ...

Beyond ASCII, a Python string is a sequence of Unicode code points, and ord can return values far above 127. See ord() and chr(). This question sticks to ASCII so that every language agrees on what one character is.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

"Have I seen this before?": hash tables

One way to check for repeats is to compare every character with every other one. That works, but for a string of n characters it takes about n×n comparisons.

So checking whether a value is already there takes about the same short time however much is stored: constant time on average. (Two values can land in the same slot, which is why it's "on average".) Going through the string once, checking and remembering each character, takes about n steps.

Python's hash table: set

A set holds each value at most once:

seen = set()
seen.add("x")
"x" in seen      # True
"y" in seen      # False
seen.add("x")    # already there: nothing changes
len(seen)        # 1

Sets work by hashing, which is why their elements must be hashable. Strings are. See Set Types in the Python documentation. (A dict is the same idea with a value stored for each key.)
learning.cpp:
Characters are numbers: ASCII

A computer stores each character as a number, its character code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is the oldest common set of codes. It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

A few landmarks are worth knowing:

  32       space
  48 – 57  '0' to '9'
  65 – 90  'A' to 'Z'
  97 – 122 'a' to 'z'

So 'A' (65) and 'a' (97) are different characters: they're 32 apart. Digits and letters are in order, so subtracting codes gives positions: 'c' minus 'a' is 2.

In C++, a char already is a small integer, so you can use it in arithmetic directly or convert it explicitly:

static_cast<int>('a');   // 97
static_cast<char>(65);   // 'A'
'c' - 'a';                // 2
for (char c : s) { ... }  // c is each character of s

Beyond ASCII, a std::string is just a sequence of bytes, and whether char is signed is up to the compiler, so codes above 127 may come out negative. This question sticks to ASCII (0 to 127), where none of that matters.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

"Have I seen this before?": hash tables

One way to check for repeats is to compare every character with every other one. That works, but for a string of n characters it takes about n×n comparisons.

A hash table remembers what it has seen. It turns each value into a number, its hash, which picks a slot to store it in. So checking whether a value is already there takes about the same short time however much is stored: constant time on average. (Two values can land in the same slot, which is why it's "on average".) Going through the string once, checking and remembering each character, takes about n steps.

C++'s hash table: std::unordered_set

An unordered_set holds each value at most once. On this site <unordered_set> is already included and using namespace std; is in effect. In your own programs, add #include <unordered_set>.

unordered_set<char> seen;
seen.insert('x');
seen.count('x');   // 1: it's there
seen.count('y');   // 0: it isn't
auto [where, added] = seen.insert('x');  // added is false: already there
seen.size();       // 1

The C++ standard says "Unordered associative containers provide an ability for fast retrieval of data based on keys. The worst-case complexity for most operations is linear, but the average case is much faster" (working draft, [unord.req]; the ISO standard itself is sold, not published free). cppreference is a friendlier guide. (unordered_map is the same idea with a value stored for each key.)
learning.java:
Characters are numbers: ASCII

A computer stores each character as a number, its character code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is the oldest common set of codes. It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

A few landmarks are worth knowing:

  32       space
  48 – 57  '0' to '9'
  65 – 90  'A' to 'Z'
  97 – 122 'a' to 'z'

So 'A' (65) and 'a' (97) are different characters: they're 32 apart. Digits and letters are in order, so subtracting codes gives positions: 'c' minus 'a' is 2.

In Java, s.charAt(i) gives the char at index i. A char is a number underneath, so a cast gives its code:

(int) 'a';                      // 97
(char) 65;                      // 'A'
'c' - 'a';                      // 2
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) { ... }  // c is each character of s

Beyond ASCII, a Java char is a UTF-16 code unit (0 to 65535), and some characters (such as many emoji) take two. This question sticks to ASCII, where one character is always one char.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

"Have I seen this before?": hash tables

One way to check for repeats is to compare every character with every other one. That works, but for a string of n characters it takes about n×n comparisons.

A hash table remembers what it has seen. It turns each value into a number, its hash, which picks a slot to store it in. So checking whether a value is already there takes about the same short time however much is stored: constant time on average. (Two values can land in the same slot, which is why it's "on average".) Going through the string once, checking and remembering each character, takes about n steps.

Java's hash table: HashSet

A HashSet holds each value at most once. It lives in java.util, so put the import lines above class Solution:

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

Set<Character> seen = new HashSet<>();
seen.add('x');        // true: it was added
seen.add('x');        // false: already there
seen.contains('y');   // false
seen.size();          // 1

A set holds objects, not primitives like char, so Java converts each char to a Character for you. That's called autoboxing (JLS §5.1.7).

The documentation says: "This class implements the Set interface, backed by a hash table (actually a HashMap instance)", and "offers constant time performance for the basic operations (add, remove, contains and size), assuming the hash function disperses the elements properly among the buckets" (HashSet, Java 21). (HashMap is the same idea with a value stored for each key.)
learning.d:
Characters are numbers: ASCII

A computer stores each character as a number, its character code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is the oldest common set of codes. It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

A few landmarks are worth knowing:

  32       space
  48 – 57  '0' to '9'
  65 – 90  'A' to 'Z'
  97 – 122 'a' to 'z'

So 'A' (65) and 'a' (97) are different characters: they're 32 apart. Digits and letters are in order, so subtracting codes gives positions: 'c' minus 'a' is 2.

In D, indexing a string gives a char, which is a number underneath, so a cast gives its code:

cast(int) 'a';     // 97
cast(char) 65;     // 'A'
'c' - 'a';         // 2
foreach (c; s) { ... }  // c is each char of s

Beyond ASCII, a D string is UTF-8, and one character can take several chars. (foreach (dchar c; s) decodes whole characters.) This question sticks to ASCII, where one character is always one char.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

"Have I seen this before?": hash tables

One way to check for repeats is to compare every character with every other one. That works, but for a string of n characters it takes about n×n comparisons.

A hash table remembers what it has seen. It turns each value into a number, its hash, which picks a slot to store it in. So checking whether a value is already there takes about the same short time however much is stored: constant time on average. (Two values can land in the same slot, which is why it's "on average".) Going through the string once, checking and remembering each character, takes about n steps.

D's hash table: associative arrays

D has no separate set type built in. Its associative arrays are hash tables, built into the language. An associative array from char to bool works as a set:

bool[char] seen;
seen['x'] = true;
if ('x' in seen) { ... }   // true: it's there
if ('y' in seen) { ... }   // false: it isn't
seen.length;               // 1

(in actually gives a pointer to the stored value, or null if the key isn't there, which is why it works in an if.) See Associative Arrays in the D language specification.

description.javascript:
Implement an algorithm to determine if a string has all unique characters.

Given a string s, return true if no character appears in it more than once, and false otherwise. Upper-case and lower-case letters are different characters, and a space counts as a character too.

New to this? The tab covers ASCII characters and Set.
